subject: Warning step failure, high deviance explained but no

messages.author: 9635782afb89a6e3
messages.subject: Warning step failure, high deviance explained but no
parts:
Hello to all,

I wish to run DSM analyses on several bird species. However, I have a high percentage of zeros in my data, and I get the following warning when I try to run the dsm function:

Warning message: In newton(lsp = lsp, X = G$X, y = G$y, Eb = G$Eb, UrS = G$UrS, L = G$L, : Fitting terminated with step failure - check results carefully

1. My first question is : what can be done about this warning? I have seen contrasted  opinions on this warning online, and I would like to know whether the models leading to this warning could be considered, after checking model plots, or should they be discarded based on this warning?

2. Then, when I look at the summary from my models containing a double smoothed effect of coordinates X and Y (even those WITHOUT the previous warning message I mentioned), I am very surprised to see that the p-value is not significant, and yet, the deviance explained is really high! This makes me doubt the model is valid. I have several outliers in my dataset, which I cannot delete because they were correctly sampled, and I suspect they may be responsible for this weird result. Do you have any opinions on this?

Family: Negative Binomial(0)
Link function: log Formula: Nhat ~ s(x, y, k = 10) + offset(off.set)
Parametric coefficients:
                    Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept) -23.57        20.96       -1.125    0.261

Approximate significance of smooth terms:
            edf Ref.df Chi.sq p-value
s(x,y)    2       2 1.      19       0.551
R-sq.(adj) = -215 Deviance explained = 71.3% -REML = 16.093 Scale est. = 1 n = 893

3. Lastly, I know that Hurdle models can be used to handle a high proportion of zeros in data, but I did not find any example of the use of Hurdle models in dsm, except for a project led by Filippo Franchini to build a new package integrating Hurdle models. Could you tell me if there are any other ways that I may have missed? Or alternatively, what can be done in case of a zero inflation, as I also saw that integrating ziplss into dsm models is rather complicated from a previous post (https://groups.google.com/g/distance-sampling/c/oj1j8mSmnTc/m/sg9NC4PAhDwJ)?

Many thanks for your help, and I wish you all a very nice day,

Delphine

messages.author: 350dad0a615d36db
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Warning step failure, high deviance explained but no
parts:
Hi Delphine, hi listfolk,

Thanks for providing the summary() result, this makes things easier to
diagnose, though I don't want to claim this is the real answer without
poring over the resulting model, I think it is fair to say you shouldn't
use the results provided by this model. There are a number of red flags
here as well as the warning message:

- The negative binomial parameter is estimated as 0. From the ?mgcv::nb
manual page, we know that the variance of this model is estimated as
var(y) = mu + mu^2/theta, where mu is the model mean and theta is the
parameter you estimate as 0. So we have a model with infinite variance
here (mu + mu/0 = mu + Inf = Inf), that's certainly a warning sign that
something has gone wrong.

- Your spatial smooth has only 2 estimated degrees of freedom. This most
likely means that the model form is incorrect (abundance doesn't vary in
space or k is too small, maybe?).

- The R^2 is a large negative number. Though R^2 is generally not that
useful (and you shouldn't perform model selection using it), having it
be large and negative is a sign something has gone wrong.

So to your first question: yes discard this model.

As to what to do about it: it's somewhat hard to diagnose from a
distance (please feel free to send me code/data off-list if that would
be helpful, but before you do...) It's worth checking to see if there is
some issue with your data setup, a significant amount of times these
issues are down to some problem in the setup of the tables etc rather
than a "true" issue with the data collected. The model object you have
will have a $data element. Inspecting this (specifically the Nhat and
Sample.Label columns) will let you check whether you have an issue with
how dsm is interpreting the data you gave it. Another potential issue
might be that the offset is being calculated in the incorrect units.

On hurdle-type models, I've not spend any additional time thinking about
this since the last post on this topic. The implementation is relatively
fiddly and I'm sure of the situations in which it's useful (vs Tweedie
or negbin). It probably requires some serious thought as to how this
meshes with the distance sampling part of the model.


Hope this helps.
--dave

messages.author: 350dad0a615d36db
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Warning step failure, high deviance explained but no
parts:
Just to come back to this. Delphine and I corresponded off-list and I
had a look at her data. The issue was that the Sample.Labels did not
match for the bulk of the observations. This lead to only 2 non-zero
segment counts.

You can check this by looking at model$data$count or
model$data$abundance.est to see what the computed response values are.

I'll look at putting-in some better checks in the future so dsm can warn
you if this happens.

best,
--dave
